headline: California Returns Sacred Coastal Lands to Three Tribal Nations
meta_description: After 18 years of advocacy, three Coastal Yuki tribes regain 136 acres of Northern California coastline, including the ancestral village site of K'etim.
summary_short: Three tribal nations have reclaimed 55 hectares of Northern California coastline, including Blues Beach and the ancestral village of K'etim, in Caltrans' first-ever land…
body:
After nearly two decades of persistent advocacy, three Coastal Yuki tribal nations have officially reclaimed 136 acres of Northern California coastline—marking the first time California's transportation department has ever returned land to Indigenous ownership. The deed, recorded on July 6, transferred the property to Kai Poma, a nonprofit founded by representatives of the Coyote Valley Band of Pomo Indians, the Round Valley Indian Tribes, and the Sherwood Valley Band of Pomo Indians. The land includes Blues Beach and K'etim, a major village site whose name comes from a creation story about Seaweed Woman and Coyote shaping the coastline and its people.

The journey began in 2005, when tribal leaders learned that looters were excavating K'etim's archaeological sites and exposing ancestral remains. After years of requests went unanswered, Senator Mike McGuire authored Senate Bill 231 in 2021, specifically authorizing the transfer at no cost. "We always felt this was ours," said Eddie Knight, chairman of Kai Poma and a Coastal Yuki descendant. "It may have been owned privately by somebody, but we still knew it was ours."

The property—situated about 187 miles north of San Francisco—comprises half a mile of beach, 100 acres of terrace holding archaeological sites, and 40 acres of sloping land where the tribes can build. The tribes plan to construct a traditional roundhouse, hold ceremonies, and establish educational programs teaching youth about harvesting native foods, seafood, and traditional ecological knowledge. The beach will remain open to the public at no charge, as required by law. Kai Poma has already secured a grant for an archaeological survey and is planning a celebration ceremony for all eight bands in Mendocino County. This transfer is part of California's broader Land Back movement, which has returned tens of thousands of acres to tribes in recent years.
quick_facts: 136 acres of coastal land returned to three tribal nations
First-ever Caltrans land transfer to Indigenous ownership
K'etim village site protected after 18 years of tribal advocacy
Located near Westport, California, 187 miles north of San Francisco
Beach remains open to public under new tribal stewardship
